summary: The Climate Case Files is a free web game and data tool that turns climate trends into detective work. Players investigate three cases in Mexico (a storm on the Veracruz coast, rising heat in Pachuca, a cold snap in Monterrey) with a clock running, and every decision costs hours. To choose well, they open the Detective’s Archive: pick any place on Earth, a variable and a time period, and the tool pulls NASA POWER monthly data from 1981 and draws the series. It then runs a Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s slope, reports a p-value, and says whether the change is a real trend or just natural variation. A hunch mode asks users to guess before seeing the result. Data are gridded, so they show regional trends, not conditions on a single street. We built it because many people hear climate claims they cannot check. Here they can test the data themselves, in a few taps, from a phone.
details:
What it does and how it works
The Climate Case Files has two parts that share the same data. The Detective’s Archive lets anyone pick a place on Earth, a variable (mean, maximum or minimum temperature, rainfall, humidity) and a time period. It downloads NASA POWER monthly data from 1981, plots the series, and runs a Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s slope to say whether there is a real trend or only natural variation. The game uses the same tool: three cases in Mexico (Veracruz coast, Pachuca, Monterrey) where each decision costs hours, so players must read the data to protect their community. Each case has 7 endings and a bronze, silver or gold medal.

Benefits and intended impact
It lets people test a climate claim themselves, in a few taps on a phone, with no account and no install. We hope it helps students and families see the difference between a trend and a single hot or cold year. It is free, public and works offline after the first visit.

Tools
HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, with no backend. NASA POWER API for data. Web Audio API for generated music, so there are no copyright issues. Service worker for offline use. Playwright and axe-core for automated tests, and SciPy and pymannkendall to check our statistics. Hosted on GitHub Pages. Code and text were written with help from Claude, and the illustrations were generated with AI.

What is creative
Climate data becomes a detective story with a clock. A hunch mode asks players to guess the trend before they see it, and the climate stripes in the game are drawn from real Pachuca data.

What we took into account
Honest limits: the data are gridded, so they show regional trends, not one street. Accessibility (automated checks found no violations), mobile-first design, English and Spanish versions, and no images of minors.
